        MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS IN SUPPORT OF
                THE MISO TRANSMISSION OWNERS

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the MISO Transmission Owners2

submit this motion to intervene and comments in support of the October 2, 2026 Filing by

the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) in which MISO proposes

 revisions to its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff

(“Tariff”) to establish a Large Load Addition Resource Study (“LARS”) process.3 As

detailed in the LARS Filing, the LARS process provides a streamlined and flexible process

whereby MISO is able to expedite the study of load interconnection requests of 200

megawatts (“MW”) or greater that are paired with electrically proximate new generation

resources. LARS provides an accelerated framework that will “facilitate the cost effective,

timely and reliable integration of new large loads into the system.”4

       As MISO explains, MISO’s LARS proposal is built upon MISO’s existing

Expedited Project Review (“EPR”) for load integration and the Expedited Resource

Additions Study (“ERAS”) for accelerated generation interconnection and positions the

region to meet the significant increase in electricity demand and support critically

important industries.5 LARS is aligned with initiatives such as the Department of Energy’s

(“DOE”) Speed to Power Initiative6 and is responsive to the Commission’s June 18, 2026

Show Cause Proceeding that called on MISO to address potential bottlenecks limiting the

ability of new generation and electrically proximate large loads to be studied for their

combined impacts on the transmissions system.7

        As noted in the LARS Filing, the addition of new large loads to the system has the

potential to strain the region’s resource adequacy needs, with new large load additions

coming online faster than the generation needed to support them.8 By studying the

generation and load in a parallel, coordinated, and streamlined manner, MISO’s LARS

proposal can reduce study times for both load and generation, and identify cost-effective

solutions for interconnection that are more efficient than if load and generation were

studied separately.9

       The MISO Transmission Owners support MISO’s LARS proposal. As explained

in the LARS Filing, the Commission should accept the proposed Tariff revisions, effective

December 2, 2026, to ensure new large loads paired with generation can be studied in

streamlined, efficient, and expedited manner.

I.     MOTION TO INTERVENE

       This proceeding involves revisions to MISO’s Generator Interconnection

Procedures and the Tariff that are necessary to implement LARS. Under the Commission’s

rules, intervention is appropriate where “[t]he movant has . . . an interest which may be

directly affected by the outcome of the proceeding.”10 As Transmission Owners within

MISO that are subject to the Tariff, each of the MISO Transmission Owners may be

affected by the Commission’s action in this proceeding.        MISO’s LARS proposal

specifically identifies MISO Transmission Owners as one of the four primary types of

MISO Transmission Owners has a direct interest in this case that cannot be adequately

represented by any other party. Therefore, the Commission should allow the intervention

of each MISO Transmission Owner.

II.    COMMENTS IN SUPPORT

       The MISO Transmission Owners support MISO’s LARS Filing. The LARS Filing

will provide the region with another efficient, effective, and appropriately tailored tool to

address the need to expedite the interconnection of new large loads and the necessary

generation to serve them. The proposed LARS process provides a framework to a parallel,

streamlined, and coordinated study process for pairing new load with much needed

generation projects. The pairing of new load with generation for large load customers is

part of a broader suite of efforts on the part of MISO and MISO stakeholders to address

resource adequacy and reliability needs across the MISO footprint while providing a

pathway to bring new large loads online as fast as possible. The Commission should accept




11
       LARS Filing at 6.

                                              4
 the LARS Filing, finding the LARS proposal to be a just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory or preferential solution to addressing a specifically regional problem.12

          A.     The LARS Proposal Is Just and Reasonable Given It Is Narrowly
                 Tailored in Scope, Avoids Negative Impacts on the Generator
                 Interconnection Queue, and Facilitates Speed to Power

          The LARS proposal is a narrowly tailored but valuable tool that enables the

accelerated evaluation and integration of electrically proximate large load and generation

pairs and the related identification of more efficient network upgrades.         As a new

permanent study process, the LARS proposal will provide for a new Large Load Generator

Interconnection Agreement in an estimated 120 days.13 The LARS proposal is a balanced

and necessary addition to MISO’s tools for addressing exponential load growth across the

region.

                 1.     Urgent Need to Interconnect New Large Loads and Associated
                        Generation

          MISO and MISO stakeholders, including the MISO Transmission Owners, fully

agree on the need to meet the moment by facilitating the interconnection of new large loads,

such as data centers, without jeopardizing resource adequacy and reliability needs.14 The

urgent resource adequacy and reliability needs that led to the LARS proposal are in part

due to recent, rapid changes to the MISO footprint. Specifically, recent assessments by

MISO demonstrate that a combination of factors, including, among other things, the rapid

 growth of large energy-consuming industries (i.e., data centers and manufacturing), and

early retirements of large generating units, are significantly impacting resource adequacy

and reliability needs in the region just when more generation is needed to serve new large

loads.15 For example, the 2025 Organization of MISO States-MISO Survey found that

“[a]t least 3.1 GW of additional capacity beyond the committed capacity will be needed to

meet the projected planning reserve margin forecast.”16 As noted by MISO, the LARS

proposal, along with MISO’s recent generator interconnection reforms accepted by the

Commission, such as ERAS, will speed up the study process for both new large loads and

generation, bringing new large loads and necessary generation online faster than the status

quo of studying these requests separately and in a non-coordinated manner.17

       The LARS proposal builds off of the successful EPR and ERAS processes. The

LARS load study process requires similar information to that required in the EPR process,

while the LARS generation study process builds off of ERAS.18 LARS improves upon

these two processes, however, by integrating the study and planning of new large load with

generation, thereby enabling the identification of more efficient transmission Network

 Upgrade solutions. Additionally, LARS is a permanent, rather than temporary, proposal

that will provide a long-term market signal and certainty to new large loads and generation

for at minimum 15 years by pairing new electrically proximate generation appropriately

sized to serve new large loads.19

       As shown above, the proposed LARS Filing is narrowly tailored to address speed

to power and the resource adequacy and reliability needs of the region, while addressing

the concerns outlined in the Show Cause Order, specifically, the need to pair new

generation with new large loads.

               2.      LARS Is an Appropriate, Focused, and Needed Solution to Bringing
                       on New Large Loads and Generation in a Timely Manner

       As MISO explained, the region faces the twin imperatives of bringing critically

important new large loads online fast enough while not exacerbating the region’s resource

adequacy concerns by failing to bring new generation to support these new large loads.20

The current separate, non-coordinated study processes of studying load interconnection

requests and generator interconnection requests separately was identified by MISO as a

key hurdle to speeding up the integration of large loads without compromising reliability.21

       Meeting resource adequacy and reliability needs is a paramount concern for the

MISO Transmission Owners and in MISO, it is the Load Serving Entities’ (“LSE”)

obligation to meet the load needs for most of the region’s states.22 LSEs are also typically

 the entity responsible for interconnecting new large loads that seek to take service in their

service territory.23   The LARS proposal respects the division of responsibility by

establishing a single application process that is initiated by the LARS Associated

Transmission Customer, typically the LSE.24         However, the Transmission Owners,

Interconnection Customer, and Associated Load all have critical roles to play in the LARS

Application process.25

       The LARS process is also designed to avoid disrupting MISO’s existing load and

generator interconnection study processes. First, the LARS proposal includes a robust pre-

submission coordination process aimed at streamlining the LARS Application process

prior to submittal with specific consultation requirements and timelines baked into the

process. Transmission Owners have a distinct role to play in the LARS pre-submission

coordination process by meeting with an Interconnection Customer that proposes to

interconnect for participation in LARS and working jointly with that Interconnection

Customer to identify a feasible Point of Interconnection (“POI”). MISO Transmission

Owners must also provide necessary attestation with regard to an agreed upon POI with

the Interconnection Customer as a part of the LARS Application.26 Second, LARS is

limited to three study cycles per year with ten LARS Applications per cycle. This limited

window will allow for MISO to meet its stated goal of studying and completing the ten

 generation/load pairs in one model.27 Third, LARS projects will not impact existing

customers in MISO’s generator interconnection queue (the Definitive Planning Phase

process or “DPP”), with LARS requests not included in DPP studies, thereby avoiding

utilizing available transmission capacity.28 Fourth, and finally, LARS includes various

safeguards to deter customers from gaming the LARS process and speculative

applications.29 Together, these requirements ensure “commercially viable and shovel

ready projects enter LARS.”30

       The LARS proposal advances key elements of the DOE’s Speed to Power Initiative

and is responsive, in part, to the Commission’s Show Cause Order. MISO Transmission

Owners support the goals of the LARS proposal, with it building off of recent successful

MISO efforts to expedite the study and addition of new loads and generation in a timely

manner, while identifying more efficient transmission solutions.

 III.   CONCLUSION

       For these reasons, the MISO Transmission Owners request that the Commission

grant this motion to intervene and accept the LARS Filing as just and reasonable, effective

December 2, 2026.
